canonical_statement: The article reviews antimicrobial stewardship best practices, applies the global core elements of antimicrobial stewardship to antifungal stewardship, offers antifungal stewardship recommendations, and identifies future research directions.
Recommendations were formulated from a literature review and synthesis of evidence by an interdisciplinary expert panel of the Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium.

The recommendations primarily focus on invasive candidiasis and invasive aspergillosis and mainly address institutional antifungal stewardship, while noting that the principles may extend to other invasive mycoses and care settings.
The statement reports that nearly 3% of all US hospital admissions and 7.7% of ICU admissions are associated with systemic antifungal prescribing.
The statement reports that approximately 30% to 50% of antifungal prescriptions could be optimized or are inappropriate.
Antifungal stewardship activities are an essential part of a comprehensive stewardship approach in facilities where antifungals are used.
Antimicrobial stewardship and antifungal stewardship goals should be integrated into hospital strategic plans and policies with senior leadership engagement, accountability, and dedicated resources.

Core stewardship team members should have in-depth knowledge and clinical experience in invasive fungal disease epidemiology, diagnostics, antifungal pharmacokinetics, dosing, duration, surveillance, drug interactions, toxicities, and therapeutic drug monitoring, ideally including infectious diseases physicians and infectious diseases-trained pharmacists.

Antifungal stewardship teams should develop ongoing collaborative strategies with practitioners who frequently manage invasive fungal disease or include specialists from high-prescribing specialties as core participants in antifungal stewardship discussions.
Centers that frequently manage invasive fungal disease should have access to timely conventional and non-culture-based diagnostic testing for Candida and Aspergillus species.

Targeted education should be incorporated into a multifaceted antifungal stewardship program to address interpretation of microbiology results, colonization versus infection, prophylaxis versus empiric therapy, and antifungal dosing and monitoring.
Whenever possible, infectious diseases consultation should be performed for patients with invasive fungal diseases such as fungemia, invasive aspergillosis, mucormycosis, and cryptococcal meningitis.

Institutions should develop care pathways or treatment bundles and guidelines so that diagnostic and therapeutic interventions for invasive fungal disease are delivered in a timely and logical sequence.
Ongoing interventions such as handshake stewardship rounds or postprescription review and feedback should be considered essential components of comprehensive antifungal stewardship.
Facilities should systematically evaluate the quality of antifungal prescribing and use data-driven strategies to optimize antifungal stewardship interventions.
Additional research is needed to develop and evaluate tools that facilitate antifungal stewardship while maximizing impact and minimizing resource requirements.
Centers managing patients with invasive fungal disease should establish or adapt local surveillance systems for fungal infections to support antifungal stewardship initiatives.
Centers routinely managing invasive fungal disease should have access to timely antifungal susceptibility testing.
Centers that routinely perform antifungal susceptibility testing should develop cumulative antifungal susceptibility reports, although evidence for their antifungal stewardship utility is limited.

Antifungal stewardship should promote rational diagnostic testing, and results from fungal cultures and non-culture-based tests should be communicated to stewardship teams to facilitate real-time interventions.
Medication records should be screened by a clinical pharmacist or clinician for antifungal drug interactions, including when concomitant medications are started or stopped.
Centers routinely managing invasive fungal disease should have access to timely therapeutic drug monitoring for triazole antifungal agents.
All facilities should have a mechanism to track antifungal drug use.
Benchmarking antifungal use can support antifungal stewardship work.
Antifungal stewardship programs should assess patient-level outcomes where possible.
All antifungal stewardship programs should have a mechanism for direct data feedback to prescribers.
For serum (1→3)-β-D-glucan for Candida, Table 1 reports 80% sensitivity and 80% specificity; PPV/NPV are 9%/>99% at 2% prevalence, 30%/97% at 10% prevalence, and <63%/90% at 30% prevalence.
For serum mannan/anti-mannan for Candida, Table 1 reports 58% sensitivity and 93% specificity; PPV/NPV are 12.5%/99% at 2% prevalence, 50%/95% at 10% prevalence, and 77%/83% at 30% prevalence.
For blood T2Candida, Table 1 reports 91% sensitivity and 98% specificity; PPV/NPV are 0.5%/>99% at 2% prevalence, 81%/99% at 10% prevalence, and 96.4%/96% at 30% prevalence.
For Candida PCR, Table 1 reports 73% sensitivity and 95% specificity; PPV/NPV are 16.7%/99% at 2% prevalence, 50%/94% at 10% prevalence, and 74%/81% at 30% prevalence.
For Aspergillus galactomannan, Table 1 reports 71% sensitivity and 89% specificity; PPV/NPV are 8%/99% at 2% prevalence, 41%/96% at 10% prevalence, and 72%/87% at 30% prevalence.
For serum (1→3)-β-D-glucan for Aspergillus, Table 1 reports 81% sensitivity and 78% specificity; PPV/NPV are 8%/>99% at 2% prevalence, 29%/97% at 10% prevalence, and 62%/91% at 30% prevalence.
Table 2 reports MALDI-TOF identification of bacteria and yeasts (>200 species) with about 1 minute of hands-on time and 5 minutes of turnaround time after organism recovery from blood culture.

Table 2 reports multiplex PCR blood-culture identification panels with approximately 2 minutes or less of hands-on time and 60 to 90 minutes of turnaround time after positive blood culture, with panel-dependent Candida and other organism coverage.

Table 2 reports PNA-FISH/related rapid Candida identification approaches with approximately 90-minute turnaround time after positive blood culture and assay-dependent identification of two to five Candida species.

Table 2 identifies T2 magnetic resonance as the only listed FDA-approved rapid molecular system that identifies Candida species directly from blood before a positive blood culture, with less than 5 minutes of hands-on time and 180 to 300 minutes of turnaround time.
The sample invasive candidiasis bundle calls for two high-volume blood cultures totaling 40 mL before antifungal therapy is started.

canonical_statement: The sample invasive candidiasis bundle calls for appropriate initial antifungal selection and dosing based on local epidemiology, started within 12 hours of culture.
The sample invasive candidiasis bundle calls for an ophthalmologic examination within the first week of diagnosis.
After therapy starts, the sample invasive candidiasis bundle calls for daily follow-up blood cultures until candidemia clearance is documented.
The sample invasive candidiasis bundle calls for echocardiography when fungemia or fever persists or new cardiac symptoms develop.

The sample invasive candidiasis bundle calls for reassessment of clinical efficacy 3 to 5 days after therapy starts and consideration of alternative therapy when identification and susceptibility results are available.
The sample invasive candidiasis bundle calls for at least 2 weeks of antifungal therapy after blood-culture clearance, with longer treatment when organ involvement is present.
The sample invasive candidiasis bundle calls for step-down to oral fluconazole in patients with a favorable clinical course and a documented susceptible isolate.
The sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for serum galactomannan testing repeated twice in patients who are not receiving mold-active azole prophylaxis.
The sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for CT imaging of the chest and/or sinus or brain when symptoms localize to those sites.
The sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for bronchoscopy within 48 hours with BAL cytology, culture, and galactomannan testing, with transbronchial biopsy if feasible.
The sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for appropriate initial antifungal selection and dosing considering prior antifungal exposure and local epidemiology.
The sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for systematic drug-interaction screening whenever a triazole antifungal is started or stopped.
After therapy starts, the sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for periodic, for example weekly, serum galactomannan testing as an adjunct to treatment-response assessment.
The sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for therapeutic drug monitoring of voriconazole and posaconazole and possibly isavuconazole to document adequate drug exposure.
The sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for reassessment of therapy appropriateness using microbiological, culture, or histological results.
The sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for repeat chest CT after 3 to 4 weeks and periodically thereafter based on clinical response.
The sample invasive aspergillosis bundle calls for step-down to an oral triazole in patients with a favorable clinical course.

Table 4 classifies as essential antifungal stewardship activities: institutional prophylaxis/empiric-treatment pathways or bundles, targeted education, antifungal drug-interaction review, handshake rounds or postprescription review and feedback, intravenous-to-oral transition programs, and local surveillance/reporting of invasive fungal disease.

Table 4 classifies as achievable antifungal stewardship activities: rapid non-culture diagnostics communicated to clinicians, timely susceptibility testing, microbiology-report therapy/dosing comments, cumulative susceptibility reports, timely therapeutic drug monitoring, and systematic review of autopsy reports and outcomes for missed or undertreated invasive fungal disease.

Table 4 classifies as aspirational antifungal stewardship activities: regional or national surveillance participation, individualized patient-risk assessment, optimized point-of-care microbiological testing, personalized therapeutic-drug-monitoring dose adaptation such as Bayesian methods, and advanced radiologic approaches for invasive aspergillosis.

Table 5 lists example antifungal stewardship performance measures including mortality or fungal-free survival, length of stay, clinical response, appropriateness of antifungal choice/dose/route/duration, time to optimal therapy, guideline adherence, culture clearance, recurrence or breakthrough infection, completion of quality measures, and therapeutic drug monitoring with achievement of target levels.

The statement reports that a nine-component invasive candidiasis management bundle used in 648 nonneutropenic candidemia patients across 11 regional medical centers was associated with clinical success of 92.9% with bundle compliance versus 75.8% without compliance (P=.011).
The statement reports that handshake stewardship rounds in a children’s hospital were associated with a 12.1% decrease in antifungal days of therapy, from 131 to 109 DOT per 1000 patient-days.
The statement reports that integrating beta-D-glucan testing with a designated ICU stewardship champion reduced inappropriate initiation of antifungal therapy by 90% in one described strategy.
The statement reports that antifungal drug-drug interactions occurred in approximately 88% of hospitalizations in which mold-active triazoles were administered.
The statement reports that antifungal agents, particularly fluconazole, were routinely underdosed in about one-third of patients with sepsis in a pharmacokinetic point-prevalence study.

The statement identifies five key surveillance elements for invasive fungal disease: standardized case definitions, defined populations for continuous monitoring, species-level identification of cultured fungi when possible, real-time mechanisms for reporting/analyzing/disseminating data to prescribers, and incentives for conducting surveillance.

The statement identifies days of therapy and defined daily dose as the two primary antifungal drug-use metrics; DOT is described as preferred in the United States, whereas DDD is widely used in Europe.

The statement describes the NHSN standardized antibiotic administration ratio as observed antifungal days of therapy divided by risk-adjusted expected days of therapy, with values greater than 1 indicating more use than predicted; antifungal agents targeting invasive candidiasis were added to the metric in the 2019 update.
The performance of non-culture-based fungal diagnostic tests can vary by host characteristics, type of immunosuppression, specimen type, and concomitant medications or treatments.

The statement notes that data evaluating cumulative antifungal susceptibility reports for antifungal stewardship are limited and that no specific standards have been proposed for constructing or analyzing antifungal cumulative susceptibility reports.
Evidence that antifungal stewardship programs improve mortality, hospital length of stay, or ICU length of stay is described as largely limited to single-center experiences with variable outcomes.
The authors conclude that formal antimicrobial stewardship principles can and should extend to antifungal agents and to prevention and management of invasive fungal disease.

The authors conclude that antifungal stewardship programs can provide a foundation for improved communication, diagnosis, and invasive fungal disease management while optimizing outcomes and cost-effectiveness, but implementation requires local tailoring to healthcare systems and practices.

Table 6 presents a future antifungal stewardship research agenda spanning leadership and staffing, multidisciplinary accountability, telemedicine and diagnostic access, education, stopping rules and ambulatory stewardship, AI and natural language processing, susceptibility methods, quality scorecards, clinician apps, postimplementation quality improvement, and systematic study of stewardship failures.

The supplement was sponsored by the Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Center; the acknowledgments also note support for D. P. Kontoyiannis from the Texas 4000 Distinguished Professorship for Cancer Research and an NCI Cancer Center CORE support grant.

The authors disclosed numerous research grants, consulting relationships, personal fees, advisory roles, honoraria, and other relationships with antifungal and pharmaceutical companies; all authors submitted ICMJE disclosure forms and relevant conflicts were disclosed by the editors.
